plurals.none: no plural in everyday use (Wiktionary lists the rare יַלְדֻיּוֹת)

lexemes.note: Childhood. Feminine (־וּת); used without a plural. בַּיַּלְדוּת שֶׁלִּי “in my childhood”.

profile.feeling: Memories: a village, grandparents, long summer days.

examples.tr: In my childhood I lived in a village.
He is a friend of mine from childhood.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in use: the time of life is also said with a clause, כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי יֶלֶד / יַלְדָּה “when I was a child”.

etymology.text: From יֶלֶד “child” with the abstract ending ־וּת (Wiktionary gives no etymology); the ending also in נַעֲרוּת “youth” and בַּגְרוּת “maturity”.

funFacts: The school-leaving exam is the בַּגְרוּת, the “maturity” — the same ending ־וּת on another root.
pitfalls: Feminine, like every noun in ־וּת: יַלְדוּת יָפָה, יַלְדוּת מְאֻשֶּׁרֶת.
With בְּ and the article: בַּיַּלְדוּת (the י keeps the doubling of the article).
subtleties: About oneself people often prefer the clause כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי יֶלֶד / יַלְדָּה to the noun.

root.none: a reduplicated stem (צַעֲ־צוּעַ); Wiktionary gives no root

pattern.none: a reduplicated stem, not one of the common patterns

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

profile.feeling: A box of toys on the floor of a child’s room.

examples.tr: The boy is playing with the new toy.
We bought him a toy for his birthday.

synonyms.nuance: “a game” — also a toy that is a game (a puzzle, a board game)

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology for צַעֲצוּעַ “a toy; a decoration”; the related verb צִעְצֵעַ “to decorate” (Wiktionary) has the same doubled stem. In the Bible צַעֲצֻעִים are carved figures.

funFacts: The word is built by repeating a syllable: tsa-’a-tsu-a.
pitfalls: The final ע takes a furtive patach: tsa’atsúa.
Playing with a toy: מְשַׂחֵק בְּ / עִם צַעֲצוּעַ.
subtleties: Wiktionary also gives “a decoration”, an older use; today the word means a toy.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: A game; a match. From שׂ־ח־ק (שִׂחֵק “to play”). Construct מִשְׂחַק.

profile.feeling: Children in the yard, a board game on a rainy day, a football match on TV.

examples.tr: We watched the match on TV.
The match ended in a draw.

synonyms.nuance: “a competition, contest” — a whole event; a מִשְׂחָק is one game or match

etymology.text: From the root שׂ־ח־ק “play, laugh” in the pattern מִקְטָל (Wiktionary); the verb is שִׂחֵק “to play”.

funFacts: The same root in the Bible means “to laugh”; a game is, at heart, something to laugh at.
pitfalls: The ש is שׂ (s): mis-chák.
In the construct the second vowel shortens: מִשְׂחַק כַּדּוּרֶגֶל, plural מִשְׂחֲקֵי מַחְשֵׁב.
subtleties: מִשְׂחָק is also an actor’s acting (the verb שִׂחֵק means “to act” too).
The game and the match are one word: context decides.

verbalNoun.none: the verbal noun שִׂחוּק is rare; the noun in use is מִשְׂחָק “game”

lexemes.note: To play. Pi‘el of שׂ־ח־ק: past שִׂחֵק / שִׂחַקְתִּי (full spelling שיחק), present מְשַׂחֵק, future יְשַׂחֵק, infinitive לְשַׂחֵק. Music: נִגֵּן.

profile.feeling: Children running in the garden, a ball, a game of cards.

senses.def: to play (a game, a sport, with toys, with someone)

examples.tr: The children are playing in the garden.

examples.text: כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי יֶלֶד, שִׂחַקְתִּי כָּל הַיּוֹם בַּחוּץ.
examples.tr: When I was a child, I played outside all day.

synonyms.nuance: not a synonym but the partner: playing music, an instrument (נִגֵּן בִּפְסַנְתֵּר)

etymology.text: Pi‘el of the root שׂ־ח־ק (Wiktionary gives no etymology; its senses are “to play” and “to act”). In the Bible the root also means “to laugh” (שְׂחוֹק “laughter”).

funFacts: An actor is a שַׂחְקָן and a player a שַׂחְקָן too — the same word for the stage and the pitch.
pitfalls: Music is not שִׂחֵק: “to play the piano” is נִגֵּן בִּפְסַנְתֵּר.
Games and sports are a bare object (שִׂחֵק כַּדּוּרֶגֶל, שַׁחְמָט); a toy or a ball takes בְּ (שִׂחֵק בְּכַדּוּר); a partner takes עִם.
The ח cannot be doubled, so the past keeps i without dagesh: שִׂחֵק (full spelling שיחק).
subtleties: Wiktionary’s second sense is “to act” (in a play, a film): הִיא מְשַׂחֶקֶת בַּתֵּאַטְרוֹן.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: To grow up; to grow. A stative pa‘al: present גָּדֵל / גְּדֵלָה, future יִגְדַּל, infinitive לִגְדֹּל (full spelling לגדול). Raising (children, plants) is the pi‘el גִּדֵּל.

profile.feeling: Pencil marks on a door frame; a village childhood; tomatoes in the garden.

senses.def: to grow, get bigger (plants, children, a city, numbers)

examples.tr: The children have grown up so fast!
The tree has grown a lot.

collocations.tr: grew up in a big family

etymology.text: From the root ג־ד־ל, the root of גָּדוֹל “big” (lesson 16): to grow is “to become big”. Wiktionary’s first sense is “to be big, great”.

funFacts: The same root gives גֹּדֶל “size” and מִגְדָּל “tower” — a “big” building.
pitfalls: Raising children is the pi‘el גִּדֵּל: הִיא גִּדְּלָה שְׁלוֹשָׁה יְלָדִים; גָּדַל is growing up yourself.
The present is like an adjective (a stative verb): גָּדֵל, גְּדֵלָה (Wiktionary) — not *גּוֹדֵל.
The future has a: יִגְדַּל, תִּגְדְּלִי.
subtleties: גָּדַל and גָּדוֹל share the root: הוּא גָּדַל “he grew up”, הוּא גָּדוֹל “he is big”.

lexemes.note: To remember. Pa‘al with o in the future: יִזְכֹּר (full spelling יזכור), infinitive לִזְכֹּר (לזכור). “I remember” is the present אֲנִי זוֹכֵר.

profile.feeling: An old photograph, a name on the tip of the tongue.

examples.text: אֲנִי זוֹכֵר אֶת הַבַּיִת שֶׁל סָבָא.

synonyms.nuance: “to recall, suddenly remember” — a moment of remembering (נִזְכַּרְתִּי שֶׁ…)

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic ذَكَرَ (ḏakara) (Wiktionary). From the same root: זִכָּרוֹן “memory” and מַזְכֶּרֶת “souvenir”.

funFacts: Israel’s Memorial Day is יוֹם הַזִּכָּרוֹן, “the day of remembrance” — the same root.
pitfalls: “I remember” now is the present: אֲנִי זוֹכֵר — the past זָכַרְתִּי means “I remembered (then)”.
Reminding is another binyan: הִזְכִּיר — זֶה מַזְכִּיר לִי … “it reminds me of …”.
Do not confuse זָכַר “remembered” with the noun זָכָר “male” (Wiktionary): the second vowel differs.
subtleties: A definite object takes אֶת: זוֹכֵר אֶת הַשֵּׁם; a fact takes שֶׁ: אֲנִי זוֹכֵר שֶׁ…

verbalNoun.none: Wiktionary lists no verbal noun in use

lexemes.note: To forget. Pa‘al with a final ח: present שׁוֹכֵחַ / שׁוֹכַחַת, future יִשְׁכַּח, infinitive לִשְׁכֹּחַ (full spelling לשכוח).

profile.feeling: Keys left on the table, a name gone from memory.

senses.def: to forget (something; to do something: + infinitive)

examples.tr: I forgot the key at home.

phrases.meaning: a vow never to forget one’s home

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; “it slipped my mind” is the idiom פָּרַח מִזִּכְרוֹנִי, literally “it flew from my memory”.

etymology.text: From the root שׁ־כ־ח (Wiktionary gives no etymology); the passive is נִשְׁכַּח “was forgotten” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Psalm 137 — “If I forget you, Jerusalem” — is the best-known line with this verb.
pitfalls: The final ח gives a furtive patach in the present: שׁוֹכֵחַ, and -ַחַת in the feminine: שׁוֹכַחַת.
Forgetting to do something: שָׁכַח + infinitive (שָׁכַחְתִּי לִקְנוֹת).
The future has a, not o: יִשְׁכַּח, תִּשְׁכַּח (because of the ח).
subtleties: “Don’t forget!” is אַל + future: אַל תִּשְׁכַּח! / אַל תִּשְׁכְּחִי!

root.none: a compound of two words (גַּן + יְלָדִים): each part has its own root

pattern.none: a compound of two words, not one pattern

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

construct.none: a compound of two words: it is not put into the construct again (“the … of …” is said with שֶׁל)

lexemes.note: Kindergarten. A compound: the article goes on the second word (גַּן הַיְלָדִים); in speech usually just הַגַּן.

override.N;PL;INDF: Wiktionary joins the compound with a maqaf (גַּנֵּי־יְלָדִים); the course writes compounds with a space, as בָּתֵּי סֵפֶר.

profile.feeling: Small chairs, songs, a sandpit and a nursery teacher called by her first name.

examples.tr: In kindergarten they sing and play.
The kindergarten is close to the house.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday short form: הַיְּלָדִים בַּגַּן — Wiktionary lists it as an ellipsis; גַּן alone is also “garden”
the compulsory last year of kindergarten, at about five
a day-care centre for babies and toddlers (מְעוֹן יוֹם)

etymology.text: Calque of German Kindergarten (Wiktionary): גַּן “garden” + יְלָדִים “children”.

funFacts: The teacher is a גַּנֶּנֶת (or a גַּנָּן) — named after the “garden”.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: גַּן הַיְלָדִים “the kindergarten”; the plural changes the first: גַּנֵּי יְלָדִים.
After בְּ / לְ the ג loses its dot: בְּגַן הַיְלָדִים, לְגַן הַיְלָדִים.
subtleties: In speech the whole is usually just הַגַּן: הוּא בַּגַּן “he’s at kindergarten”.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

construct.none: not used in the construct in everyday Hebrew: “the neighbour of …” is said with שֶׁל

lexemes.note: A neighbour (a man). A woman: שְׁכֵנָה. Plural שְׁכֵנִים.

contrasts.value: a man (the plural also for a mixed group)

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses שָׁכֵן as “neighbor” (American spelling); the check does not match the course gloss “neighbour”.

profile.feeling: The stairwell of a block of flats: greetings, borrowed sugar, noise from upstairs.

senses.def: a neighbour (a man; the plural also for a mixed group)

examples.text: כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי יֶלֶד, שִׂחַקְתִּי עִם הַיְּלָדִים שֶׁל הַשְּׁכֵנִים.
examples.tr: As a child I played with the neighbours’ children.

phrases.tr: better a near neighbour than a far brother
phrases.meaning: the people close by help more than relatives far away

synonyms.nuance: someone from the same neighbourhood, not necessarily next door

etymology.text: From the root שׁ־כ־ן “to dwell”; cognate with Arabic سَكَنَ (sakana, “to reside, inhabit”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The neighbourhood is the שְׁכוּנָה — the same root “to dwell”.
pitfalls: A neighbour (person) is שָׁכֵן; the neighbourhood is שְׁכוּנָה.
A woman is a שְׁכֵנָה; a mixed group is שְׁכֵנִים.
subtleties: As an adjective שָׁכֵן means “neighbouring” (Wiktionary): מְדִינָה שְׁכֵנָה “a neighbouring country”.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

construct.none: not used in the construct in everyday Hebrew: “the neighbour of …” is said with שֶׁל

profile.feeling: The woman next door who waters your plants when you travel.

examples.tr: The neighbours (f.) sit outside in the evening.

synonyms.nuance: a woman from the same neighbourhood

etymology.text: The feminine of שָׁכֵן “neighbour” (Wiktionary lists it as its feminine counterpart); root שׁ־כ־ן “to dwell”.

funFacts: As an adjective the same form means “neighbouring”: עִיר שְׁכֵנָה “a neighbouring town”.
pitfalls: Women only: a group with one man is שְׁכֵנִים.
subtleties: The first vowel is reduced: שָׁכֵן but שְׁכֵנָה (sh’chena).

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: The (school) holidays. Masculine; הַחֹפֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל = the summer holidays. Adults’ time off is more often חֻפְשָׁה (lesson 15).

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article and keep its doubling: הַחֹפֶשׁ → (בַּ / לַ)חֹפֶשׁ; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַחֹפֶשׁ.

profile.feeling: The end of June: no school until September, the beach, the summer camp.

senses.def: the holidays, vacation — above all from school (הַחֹפֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל “the summer holidays”)

examples.tr: In the summer holidays we went to the sea.

synonyms.nuance: “a holiday, time off” — for adults, from work; a trip (יָצָאנוּ לְחֻפְשָׁה)

etymology.text: From the root ח־פ־שׁ “free” in the pattern קֹטֶל (Wiktionary, whose senses are “freedom” and “a vacation, especially from school”). From the same root: חָפְשִׁי “free” and חֻפְשָׁה “a holiday”.

funFacts: “The big holiday”, הַחֹפֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל, is what every Israeli child calls July and August.
pitfalls: Masculine — הַחֹפֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל — while חֻפְשָׁה is feminine.
The first vowel is o: chófesh (full spelling חופש).
subtleties: In set phrases חֹפֶשׁ keeps its older meaning “freedom” (Wiktionary): חֹפֶשׁ הַבִּטּוּי “freedom of expression”.

absent.reason: Hebrew has no adverb or particle for “used to”: the habitual past is a verb construction.
absent.use: הָיָה + the present form of the verb (fn.past.ongoing): הָיִיתִי מְשַׂחֵק בַּחוּץ “I used to play outside”; in formal style נָהַג + infinitive (lesson 13: הוּא נָהַג לָשֶׁבֶת כָּאן “he used to sit here”); often just the past with a word of time (תָּמִיד, כָּל יוֹם).
